result: Early clusters of nodal proteins appear before heminodes and nodes during peripheral nerve myelination, representing the earliest stage of node assembly. Temporal quantification in vitro and in vivo demonstrates that early clusters peak at 5-10 days after myelination induction, preceding the appearance of heminodes and nodes, and then decline as more mature structures form.
evaluation: Claims C4, C12, C19, C21, C86-C93, C154, and C155 collectively demonstrate through temporal quantification (Figure 6) that early clusters appear first, peak when heminodes/nodes begin forming, then decline. This temporal relationship is shown both in vitro (microfluidic cultures) and in vivo (P1, P3, P5 sciatic nerves), with appropriate controls and statistical analysis. The sequential appearance in somal-to-distal direction further supports developmental progression.

result: Formation of early clusters in the PNS requires neuronal neurofascin 186 (Nfasc186), distinguishing them from CNS early clusters which do not require neurofascins. Early clusters are barely detectable in Nfasc-/- neurons (0.21±0.05 vs 25.40±5.60 per 100 neurons in WT, p=0.0107), while glial Nfasc155 plays no role.
evaluation: Claims C6, C24, C39-C41, and C132 are well-supported by experiments comparing Nfasc+/+ and Nfasc-/- neurons co-cultured with WT Schwann cells. The statistically significant reduction (p=0.0107, n=3) demonstrates Nfasc186 dependency. The presence of glial Nfasc155 without rescue confirms isoform specificity. Citation to Freeman et al. 2015 appropriately contrasts with CNS findings.

result: Nodal proteins in early clusters are dynamically recruited exclusively by lateral diffusion in the axonal membrane, not by direct vesicular delivery. FRAP experiments show fluorescence recovery at early clusters, which is completely prevented by FLIP (blocking lateral diffusion), demonstrating that protein recruitment occurs via surface diffusion.
evaluation: Claims C7, C8, C23, C53, C58, C59, C133, and C134 are strongly supported by FRAP and FRAP/FLIP experiments (Figure 3). The complete prevention of recovery by FLIP directly demonstrates lateral diffusion as the exclusive mechanism. Controls showing FLIP does not affect vesicle transport (C61-C62) and nocodazole experiments with β1Nav-EGFP (C65-C67) further validate this conclusion.

result: Early clusters are mobile and can fuse with each other and with heminodes, actively contributing to node assembly. Time-lapse imaging demonstrates early clusters moving retrogradely toward heminodes at 0.88±0.03 μm/h, with 84.2±2.2% being mobile, and directly shows fusion events.
evaluation: Claims C9, C10, C32, C99, and C156 are supported by time-lapse imaging (Figures 5, 7, Videos 3-7) showing early cluster movement, fusion between early clusters, and fusion with heminodes. Quantification of movement speed and directionality (C94-C97) provides statistical support. The observation that all mobile early clusters move retrogradely toward heminodes strengthens the developmental relationship.

result: Early cluster formation requires the presence of myelinating Schwann cells. Schwann cells must be induced to myelinate with ascorbic acid; their presence alone without myelination induction is insufficient for early cluster formation.
evaluation: Claims C20, C42, C43, and C45 are supported by experiments (Figure 2A) comparing conditions with/without Schwann cells and with/without myelinating medium. The requirement for both Schwann cells AND myelination induction is clearly demonstrated with appropriate controls and statistical significance (p<0.01, p<0.0001).

result: Unlike heminodes, early clusters are not contacted by Schwann cell microvilli and lack axo-glial ultrastructural specializations. Immunostaining shows absence of microvillar markers (pERM, Dp116, radixin) at early clusters, and CLEM reveals close Schwann cell proximity without specialized junctions.
evaluation: Claims C22, C46-C49, and C148 are well-supported by immunostaining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) showing absence of microvillar markers and CLEM (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) showing no ultrastructural specializations. The contrast with heminodes/nodes where these markers are present strengthens the conclusion. Serial EM sections provide thorough structural analysis.

result: Early cluster formation is independent of paranodal axo-glial junctions. Assembly of early clusters is unaffected in Caspr-null neurons (90.2±28.3 vs 90.9±15.0 per 100 neurons, p=0.9838), and fluorescence recovery at early clusters shows no difference between Cntnap1+/+ and Cntnap1-/- conditions.
evaluation: Claims C25, C68, and C69 are supported by experiments in Caspr-null (Cntnap1-/-) neurons showing no effect on early cluster assembly (quantification with p=0.9838) or dynamics (FRAP experiments, Figure 4). This independence from paranodal junctions distinguishes early clusters from mature nodes and is consistent with the absence of axo-glial specializations.

result: The mobility of SEP-Nfasc186 at nodal structures gradually declines during maturation. FRAP experiments show highest mobility on unmyelinated axons, intermediate mobility at early clusters and heminodes, and minimal mobility at mature nodes, indicating progressive stabilization.
evaluation: Claims C52-C56 are supported by systematic FRAP experiments (Figure 3A-C) comparing all four conditions with appropriate quantification. The gradient of mobility (unmyelinated > early clusters > heminodes > nodes) is clearly demonstrated and consistent with progressive maturation. Confirmation in ex vivo triangularis sterni preparations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) strengthens the finding.

result: Heminodes are dynamic structures that rapidly exchange full-length Nfasc186 with the axonal pool, predominantly via lateral diffusion from the flanking unmyelinated axon. Asymmetric FRAP/FLIP experiments demonstrate that recovery is prevented when the unmyelinated side is photobleached.
evaluation: Claims C57, C60, C140, and C141 are supported by FRAP and asymmetric FRAP/FLIP experiments (Figure 3D, F, G) showing fluorescence recovery at heminodes and demonstrating the predominant contribution from the unmyelinated side. This represents the first direct demonstration of full-length Nfasc186 exchange at heminodes, as stated by the authors.

result: Paranodal axo-glial junctions act as diffusion barriers that stabilize mature nodes. Loss of junctions in Caspr-null mice significantly increases protein mobility at nodes but not at heminodes or early clusters. FRAP/FLIP experiments directly demonstrate that nodes without junctions can exchange proteins with the axonal pool via lateral diffusion.
evaluation: Claims C70, C71, C73-C76, C143, and C144 are strongly supported by FRAP experiments in Caspr-null mice (Figure 4) showing increased nodal mobility, and FRAP/FLIP experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) demonstrating that recovery at Caspr-null nodes is prevented by blocking lateral diffusion. FLIP alone causing fluorescence loss at Caspr-null but not WT nodes provides direct evidence for the barrier function.

result: Early clusters are mobile along axons, with 84.2±2.2% showing movement at an average speed of 0.88±0.03 μm/h. Movement is not explained by axonal extension (tracked relative to fixed landmarks), and multiple early clusters on the same axon move synchronously. All mobile early clusters move retrogradely toward the nearest heminode.
evaluation: Claims C78-C81 and C94-C97 are supported by extensive time-lapse imaging (Figure 5, Videos 3-5) with quantification of mobility percentage and speed. Tracking relative to immobile landmarks (C80) rules out axonal extension. The exclusive retrograde movement toward heminodes (C96-C97) is particularly compelling evidence for developmental contribution to node formation.

result: Early cluster movement is actin-dependent and involves myosin II. Latrunculin A treatment significantly reduces both the percentage and speed of mobile early clusters, while blebbistatin (myosin II inhibitor) significantly reduces movement speed (0.70±0.03 vs 0.99±0.09 μm/s, p=0.0233).
evaluation: Claims C82-C85 are supported by pharmacological experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) with latrunculin A and blebbistatin. Effective actin disruption is confirmed by phalloidin staining (C83). Statistical significance for blebbistatin effect (p=0.0233, n=4) supports myosin II involvement. However, the authors cannot distinguish between axonal and Schwann cell contributions to motility.

result: β1Nav-EGFP in early clusters is mobile and recovers by lateral diffusion, though with slower turnover than SEP-Nfasc186 (requiring 4 hours vs 15 minutes). Nocodazole treatment blocks vesicle transport but does not affect fluorescence recovery at early clusters, demonstrating lateral diffusion as the recruitment mechanism.
evaluation: Claims C63-C67 are supported by FRAP experiments with β1Nav-EGFP (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) showing recovery over 4 hours, and nocodazole experiments demonstrating that blocking microtubule-based transport does not prevent recovery. The slower turnover compared to Nfasc186 is appropriately noted. Controls showing nocodazole effectively blocks vesicle movement strengthen the conclusion.

result: The transgenic fusion proteins SEP-Nfasc186 and β1Nav-EGFP are appropriately targeted to the axonal membrane and serve as valid surrogate markers for nodal structures. Both proteins are diffusely distributed before myelination and become focally concentrated at nodes after myelination, colocalizing with endogenous nodal markers.
evaluation: Claims C34-C38 are supported by live imaging and immunostaining (Figure 1) showing proper localization and colocalization with AnkG and βIV-spectrin. The validation that early clusters in transgenic mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) show similar percentages to WT mice (81.7-86.7% at P1) confirms the transgenes do not artifactually alter early cluster formation.

result: FLIP does not affect microtubule-based vesicle transport. Analysis of β1Nav-EGFP+ vesicle movement before and after FRAP/FLIP shows no change in number or speed of mobile vesicles, validating that FLIP specifically blocks lateral diffusion without causing photodamage to the cytoskeleton.
evaluation: Claims C61 and C62 are supported by control experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) quantifying vesicle movement before and after FLIP. This important control validates the FRAP/FLIP methodology and rules out non-specific effects of photobleaching on cellular transport machinery.

result: Background claims establishing that voltage-gated sodium channels cluster at nodes of Ranvier for rapid conduction, that node assembly is thought to be initiated at heminodes with fusion leading to nodes, and that neurofascin proteins are essential for node formation.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C5, and C13 represent well-established background knowledge supported by extensive prior research and citations. These provide the necessary context for the study's findings but are not novel results of this work.

result: Prior observations of nodal protein complexes lacking flanking Schwann cells or myelin have been reported in various systems, and these structures can enhance conduction velocity.
evaluation: Claims C14-C18 accurately cite prior literature (Eshed-Eisenbach et al. 2020, Lambert et al. 1997, Freeman et al. 2015) establishing that similar structures have been observed before. These citations appropriately contextualize the current study's focus on characterizing these structures.

result: Background claims about redundant mechanisms of node assembly in PNS and CNS, including roles of Nfasc isoforms, gliomedin, paranodal junctions, and extracellular matrix proteins.
evaluation: Claims C26-C28 and C103-C116 accurately represent established knowledge from cited literature about node assembly mechanisms. These provide important context for understanding the significance of early clusters as an additional mechanism, but are not novel findings of this study.

result: Laminin stimulates myelination and enhances early cluster formation, as demonstrated by comparing matrigel-coated versus collagen-coated chambers.
evaluation: Claim C44 is supported by experiments shown in Figure 2A comparing different coating conditions. However, this is a methodological observation rather than a mechanistic finding about early cluster biology.

result: Background claims that mature nodes are very stable structures while heminodes and nascent nodes can exchange proteins with an axolemmal pool.
evaluation: Claims C50 and C51 cite prior literature (Zonta et al. 2011, Zhang et al. 2012, 2020) and are confirmed by the authors' FRAP experiments. These establish the context for comparing early cluster dynamics to other nodal structures.

result: The insensitivity of SEP-Nfasc186 mobility in heminodes to junctional disruption reflects the dominant contribution of lateral diffusion from the unmyelinated side that lacks an axo-glial junction.
evaluation: Claim C72 is a reasonable inference from the asymmetric FLIP experiments (C60) showing recovery predominantly from the unmyelinated side. Since heminodes have only one paranodal junction, loss of that junction would not affect recovery from the unmyelinated side.

result: Like heminodes, early cluster assembly depends on the interaction between Schwann cell-secreted gliomedin and neuronal Nfasc186, and they are not essential for node formation since nodes still form in the absence of gliomedin.
evaluation: Claims C117 and C118 are supported by the demonstrated Nfasc186 requirement (C24, C39-C41) and citation to Feinberg et al. 2010 showing nodes form without gliomedin. The gliomedin dependency is inferred from prior knowledge about its role at heminodes and its presence at early clusters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

result: The clustering activity of gliomedin is negatively regulated by proteolytic cleavage by BMP1/Tolloid-like proteases, and inhibition of these proteases enhances early cluster formation without affecting myelination or node assembly.
evaluation: Claims C119 and C120 cite Eshed-Eisenbach et al. 2020 and provide context for understanding regulation of early cluster formation. These are not findings of the current study but relevant prior work.

result: Early cluster assembly is restricted to large calibre NF200-positive axons that typically become myelinated in vivo, and early clusters do not assemble on unmyelinated C-type fibers in Remak bundles.
evaluation: Claims C121-C124 are supported by the authors' observations (stated as "data not shown" for C121) and citation to Eshed-Eisenbach et al. 2020 for C123. This specificity for myelinated axon types is consistent with early clusters being developmental intermediates in node formation.

result: CNS and PNS early clusters share many similarities including timing, molecular composition, glial factor dependence, persistence after myelination, and enhancement of conduction velocity. It is possible they share similar developmental roles.
evaluation: Claims C125-C131 appropriately cite extensive prior literature on CNS early clusters and draw parallels to the PNS structures characterized in this study. Claim C131 is appropriately cautious speculation ("it is possible") based on the documented similarities.

result: Background claims about Nav and Nfasc186 delivery to nodes, including that Nav α and β subunits can be independently delivered and might follow different routes.
evaluation: Claims C135-C139 cite prior literature and provide context for the finding that β1Nav-EGFP is recruited by lateral diffusion. Claim C139 is appropriate speculation based on the observation that the subunits can be independently delivered (C137-C138).

result: The ability of both early clusters and heminodes to exchange Nfasc186 with the unmyelinated axon is consistent with their ability to merge.
evaluation: Claim C142 is a reasonable inference connecting the dynamic properties demonstrated by FRAP (C53, C57, C60) with the observed fusion events (C10, C32). The shared mechanism of lateral diffusion provides a plausible basis for fusion.

result: The molecular interactions between Nfasc186 and other nodal proteins are not intrinsically different between mature nodes and early clusters but are modulated by axo-glial junctions. In the absence of junctions, Nfasc186 could potentially diffuse through internodal regions and exchange between adjacent nodes.
evaluation: Claim C145 is a reasonable inference from the FRAP data in Caspr-null mice showing nodes behave more like early clusters. However, claims C146 and C147 are speculation ("could, conceivably") that goes beyond the data. While plausible based on the demonstrated lateral diffusion, actual internodal diffusion or node-to-node exchange was not directly observed.

result: Schwann cell microvilli emerge at early stages of Schwann cell maturation before myelin ensheathment, and their absence at early clusters likely contributes to the dynamic properties of early clusters.
evaluation: Claim C149 cites Gatto et al. 2003 appropriately. Claim C150 is reasonable inference from the structural differences (C22, C46-C47, C148) and dynamic properties (C7, C29, C53), though the causal relationship is not directly tested.

result: This is the first documented example of long-range movement of membrane-bound protein complexes along the axon, excluding heminodes.
evaluation: Claim C151 is stated based on the authors' knowledge of the literature ("To our knowledge"). While the observation of early cluster movement is well-documented (C78-C81, C94-C97), the claim of being "first" cannot be fully verified without comprehensive literature review. The exclusion of heminodes is appropriate since their movement has been observed.

result: Schwann cells contacting early clusters appear to migrate along the axon at similar rates to early clusters, and might be responsible for early cluster motility.
evaluation: Claims C152 and C153 are based on observations stated as "data not shown" and explicitly presented as hypothesis ("we hypothesise"). While the actin-dependence (C82-C85) is consistent with Schwann cell involvement, the mechanism remains unresolved. The authors appropriately acknowledge they "cannot exclude an axon-based mechanism."

result: Neither the directionality nor the speed of early clusters was influenced by their distance from the nearest myelinated segment.
evaluation: Claim C98 is stated as "data not shown," making it impossible to evaluate the quality of the analysis or statistical support. While this observation would be consistent with the overall findings, it cannot be properly assessed without seeing the data.

result: Early clusters contribute to the development of nodes in peripheral axons and represent a Nfasc186-dependent developmental stage of node assembly that precedes heminode formation.
evaluation: Claims C11, C33, and C100 represent the main conclusions synthesizing multiple lines of evidence: temporal precedence (C4, C12, C86-C93), Nfasc186 dependency (C6, C24, C39-C41), fusion with heminodes (C10, C32, C99), and mobility toward heminodes (C96-C97). While the contribution to node development is strongly supported by fusion observations, the quantitative importance of this pathway versus heminode-only assembly cannot be determined from the data.
